## This is not a feature race

<div class="section-kicker">The comparison that matters</div>

<div class="lede">brms already owns the mature applied-regression benchmark. The question is what each architecture makes <em>cheap to add next</em>.</div>

<div class="rule"></div>

:::: {.grid-3}
::: {.card .accent-blue}
<span class="label brms">brms today</span>

**Deep, coherent Stan generation**

Distributional, nonlinear, multivariate, smooth, autocorrelated, censored, missing-data, and custom-family models—with a rich post-processing ecosystem.
:::

::: {.card .accent-teal}
<span class="label demo">BRM today</span>

**One formula, shared semantics**

The same `BRMI` is prepared once, then lowered to generated StanBlocks/Stan or a direct Turing model.
:::

::: {.card .accent-amber}
<span class="label enabled">The future axis</span>

**Where can computation vary without rewriting statistical intent?**

That is an architectural capability—not a claim that every implementation already exists.
:::
::::

::: {.notes}
Lead by taking brms seriously. It is the mature reference point, not a straw man. The comparison is deliberately about the marginal cost and coherence of future additions. “Architecture-enabled” means a seam exists and engineering is still required.

Sources: current brms overview and `brm()` reference (brms 2.23.2); BRM `docs/refactoring.md`, `docs/src/turing-backend.md`, and `docs/src/adaptive-centering.md` at accepted case revision `5ccf212831d8e3af10c9fc47305cd4dd0752c5d8` (published in merge `5ce974cec08e620bcbe0f2d54b36f3649d889dbf`).
:::

<div class="small muted" style="margin-top: 1em; text-align:center;">The invariant is the prepared statistical program. Parameter geometry and execution belong to the backend.</div>

::: {.notes}
The shared layer records data and parameter dependencies, axes, population designs, group blocks, observation semantics, term metadata, and fitted preprocessing. StanBlocks remains a generated-program backend. Turing consumes the plan directly and generates a DynamicPPL model; it does not interpret SLIC or Stan.

Demonstrated at the baseline: a 14-model Stan preservation corpus and broad focused Turing gates are recorded in the refactor brief. Exact gate receipts belong to that brief; this slide claims the architecture, not universal backend parity.
:::

## 1 · Extension can mean composition, not surgery

<div class="section-kicker">Future capability axis</div>

<div class="comparison-row header"><div></div><div>brms</div><div>BRM.jl</div></div>
<div class="comparison-row"><div><strong>Custom response</strong></div><div>Excellent supported route: `custom_family()` + Stan functions + R post-processing hooks.</div><div>Callable Julia distribution/factory survives preparation; Turing can execute it directly. StanBlocks adds an explicit translation.</div></div>
<div class="comparison-row"><div><strong>New term</strong></div><div>Extend formula/parser/code generation, or inject Stan with `stanvar()`.</div><div>Add a typed prepared record; implement backend methods only where execution exists.</div></div>
<div class="comparison-row"><div><strong>Composition</strong></div><div>Large built-in grammar; custom pieces must integrate with generated Stan and downstream methods.</div><div>Prepared callables, evidence wrappers, weights, links, and terms compose before backend lowering.</div></div>

:::: {.grid-2 style="margin-top: 0.7em;"}
::: {.card .accent-blue}
<span class="label brms">Fairness</span>

brms already exposes unusually strong escape hatches. Its constraint is deliberate: the executable language is Stan.
:::
::: {.card .accent-amber}
<span class="label enabled">Architecture-enabled</span>

BRM can make “native Julia first, Stan translation second” a normal extension path—but only after validation, replay, and output contracts are implemented.
:::
::::

::: {.notes}
Do not say brms is not extensible. `custom_family()` specifies distributional parameters and links; the user supplies Stan density code, and may supply R functions for `log_lik`, posterior prediction, and expected prediction. `stanvar()` can inject code into every major Stan block. The difference is the executable substrate and how many surfaces must be kept aligned.

Sources: brms `custom_family()` and `stanvar()` reference pages, both for brms 2.23.2; BRM callable-prior and complete-call translation contracts in `docs/refactoring.md`.
:::

## 2 · Structure need not fit one rectangular table

<div class="section-kicker">Future capability axis</div>

:::: {.grid-2 .wide-right}
::: {.card .accent-blue .tight}
<span class="label brms">brms strength</span>

Nonlinear formulas of arbitrary complexity, multivariate models, autocorrelation, splines/GPs, phylogenetic covariance, and custom Stan give broad structural reach.

Its primary user contract remains a formula plus a `data.frame`, with extra data/code supplied through established escape hatches.
:::

::: {.card .accent-teal .tight}
<span class="label demo">BRM demonstrated</span>

**Different axes can meet inside one model.**

$$
\begin{aligned}
C_j(t) &= \frac{D_j}{V_j}\exp\!\left(-\frac{CL_j}{V_j}t\right), \\
y_{jk} &\sim \mathcal N(C_j(t_{jk}),\sigma)
\end{aligned}
$$

`kernel(...)` evaluates one structural cell per subject; `ragged(time, subject)` joins an observation axis; formula predictors still own population and group effects.
:::
::::

<div class="small muted" style="margin-top:.75em;"><span class="label enabled">Enabled with engineering</span> State-space, ODE, renewal, and multistream models can share formula-level priors/evidence while backend-native cells own mechanics. Each new cell still needs explicit shape, AD, replay, and output support.</div>

::: {.notes}
BRM currently demonstrates this separation in the population-PK kernel, Warfarin, CDC wastewater renewal, and grey-seal integrated-population examples. The important future capability is not “arbitrary Julia” alone; it is arbitrary structural mechanics that retain formula-governed regression effects, priors, evidence, replay, and named outputs.

Fairness source: current brms nonlinear and multivariate vignettes. BRM source: `docs/src/feature-atlas.md`, `research/warfarin`, `research/wastewater`, and `research/seal`.
:::

## 3 · A backend can change the question—not the model

<div class="section-kicker">Future capability axis</div>

:::: {.grid-3}
::: {.card .accent-blue}
<span class="status stan">StanBlocks only</span>

**Generated program control**

Stan compilation, BridgeStan density access, SLIC extension hooks, descriptor-driven draw transport, and compiler-owned HSGP coordinate metadata.
:::

::: {.card .accent-violet}
<span class="status turing">Turing only</span>

**Julia-native execution**

Untranslated Julia distributions and functions, DynamicPPL model composition, native coordinate discovery, and direct access to Turing’s inference ecosystem.
:::

::: {.card .accent-teal}
<span class="status both">Both</span>

**Shared statistical contract**

Population/distributional predictors, broad priors and likelihoods, group effects, advanced terms, fitted preprocessing, replay, and the demonstrated HSGP centering transport—within stated subsets.
:::
::::

<div class="equation-panel" style="margin-top:.72em;">
<strong>Future bet:</strong> choose marginalization, HMC implementation, automatic differentiation, particles, or specialized kernels <em>after</em> model preparation—not by forking the public formula language.
</div>

::: {.notes}
This is the strongest architectural claim and should be phrased conditionally. Today’s Turing and StanBlocks lowerings do not have universal parity. Future inference methods still require implementation, tests, diagnostics, and output/replay support. The architecture makes those additions localizable; it does not supply them automatically.

brms also offers multiple inference algorithms (`sampling`, mean-field/full-rank VI, Pathfinder, Laplace, fixed-parameter) and two Stan interfaces (`rstan`, `cmdstanr`). Those are meaningful algorithm choices within one generated Stan program, and should be acknowledged if asked.
:::

## 4 · Geometry is a model implementation choice

<div class="section-kicker">Why centering belongs above handwritten code</div>

:::: {.grid-2}
::: {.equation-panel}
<span class="label demo">Centered</span>

$$
\beta_k \sim \mathcal N(0,s_k)
$$

The physical coefficient is sampled directly.

<span class="small muted">Often better when the likelihood strongly identifies the coefficient.</span>
:::

::: {.equation-panel}
<span class="label demo">Noncentered</span>

$$
z_k \sim \mathcal N(0,1),\qquad \beta_k=s_kz_k
$$

Prior scale and latent coordinate are separated.

<span class="small muted">Often better when data are weak and funnel geometry dominates.</span>
:::
::::

<div class="card accent-amber" style="margin-top:.7em; text-align:center;">
<span class="label research">The hard part</span>

The preferred coordinate can differ by group, term, frequency, and stage of adaptation. A fixed global switch throws information away.
</div>

::: {.notes}
The classic centered/noncentered tradeoff depends on information. Stan’s user guide explicitly notes noncentering tends to help when the data weakly identify the lower-level parameters, while centering can be more efficient when information is strong. Papaspiliopoulos, Roberts, and Sköld (2007) develop centered, noncentered, and partially noncentered parameterizations. Gorinova et al. (2020) demonstrates automatic partial reparameterization can avoid catastrophic choices and sometimes outperform both endpoints.
:::

## One formula; two online geometry adapters

<div class="section-kicker">Demonstrated · 133-row motorcycle case</div>

:::: {.grid-2 .wide-left}
::: {.card .accent-teal .tight .case-model}
<span class="label demo">Shared statistical model</span>

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mu(t) &= \operatorname{HSGP}_{\mu}(t),\\
\log\sigma(t) &= \operatorname{HSGP}_{\sigma}(t),\\
y(t) &\sim \mathcal N\!\left(\mu(t),\sigma(t)\right)
\end{aligned}
$$

Two same-axis HSGPs, each with eight basis frequencies. Using Normal’s standard-deviation convention, for every frequency:

$$
u_k\sim\mathcal N(0,s_k^{c_k}),\qquad
\beta_k=s_k^{1-c_k}u_k
$$

$c_k=0$ is noncentered; $c_k=1$ is centered. The physical function is unchanged.
:::

::: {.card .accent-violet .tight .case-online}
<span class="status both">Both · online</span>

**Warmup learns 16 coordinates**

- same transform, Jacobian, candidate grid, and score
- one $c_k$ per mean and log-scale basis weight
- StanBlocks discovers compiler-owned BridgeStan coordinates
- Turing discovers DynamicPPL ranges for the admitted model shape
- both call `adaptive_centering_problem` and WarmupHMC
:::
::::

<div class="case-invariant"><strong>Same target.</strong> Backend-native gradients and finite warmup trajectories may select different valid coordinates.</div>

<div class="case-provenance">Generable companion `0d00b853` · `MASS::mcycle` SHA-256 `b89a1e4…f9801` · BRM case `5ccf212`</div>

::: {.notes}
The HSGP approximation is from Riutort-Mayol et al. (2023). The translation follows the public Generable motorcycle example at immutable companion revision `0d00b8535e2c20c49017d03c7b060940eb8e7041`: all 133 `MASS::mcycle` rows, acceleration divided by its sample standard deviation, time min–max mapped to `[-1,1]`, the sine basis evaluated on `[-1.5,1.5]`, and zero-location `LogNormal(0,4)` HSGP length-scale and marginal-scale priors. The committed data come from Rdatasets revision `1dcc2bf5f955cc1224a3e1307256e1fe86b68dae` and have SHA-256 `b89a1e4eb0391a982b32be3e378df00e8593ff9971e9425e9c5d7929b74f9801`.

The shared coordinate transform and Jacobian preserve the physical target. StanBlocks uses compiler-owned coordinate metadata and BridgeStan/Enzyme target gradients. The native Turing wrapper delegates density evaluation to the exact DynamicPPL target and supplies the audited closed-form target gradient for this bounded two-HSGP Gaussian model; Enzyme differentiates the small shared coordinate transport. No BridgeStan names, indices, or draws enter the Turing path. Accepted BRM revision: `5ccf212831d8e3af10c9fc47305cd4dd0752c5d8`, published in merge `5ce974cec08e620bcbe0f2d54b36f3649d889dbf`.
:::

<div class="c-scale"><span>frequency 1</span><span>$c=0$ noncentered → $c=1$ centered</span><span>frequency 8</span></div>

:::: {.grid-2 .case-receipts}
::: {.card .accent-teal .tight}
<span class="label demo">Online receipt · each backend</span>

**133 rows · $k=8\times2$ · 20 retained draws**<br>
120-evaluation warmup · `Xoshiro(0x20260913)` · **0 divergences**
:::
::: {.card .accent-amber .tight}
<span class="label boundary">Bounded offline comparison</span>

Noncentered divergences: **31 / 29** → centered/adaptive: <strong class="nowrap">0 / 0</strong><br>
R-hat **2.04–6.64**, ESS **2.07–2.86** → **fails convergence gate**
:::
::::

::: {.notes}
The centeredness cells are the committed `results/online_centeredness.tsv` and `results/online_turing_centeredness.tsv` values. Both online runs use all 133 rows, two eight-frequency HSGPs, 20 retained draws, a 120-evaluation warmup budget, and `Xoshiro(0x20260913)`; each reports zero divergences. These are learned during warmup, not selected from or recycled from an offline pilot. Different values are expected: semantic parity means the transform, Jacobian, score, and target are preserved, not that finite backend-native trajectories select the same $c$.

The offline six-fit artifact uses four chains, 75 retained draws per chain, a 350-gradient first warmup window, and seeds `0x6a09e667:0x6a09e66a`. Centered and pilot-selected fixed geometry remove the noncentered divergences on both backends, but all maximum R-hat values are above 2 and minimum ESS values are about 2–3. It is pipeline smoke-test evidence only: do not rank coordinates or backend wall time from it. The source-faithful model uses 20 basis functions; this bounded documentation artifact uses 8.
:::

<div class="section-kicker">Future capability axis</div>

::::: {.pipeline style="grid-template-columns: 1fr .12fr 1.2fr .12fr 1.05fr;"}

<span class="small muted">levels · centers · bases · domains</span>

→

<span class="label demo">freeze</span>

**prepared state**

<span class="small muted">apply, do not silently refit</span>
:::
::: {.arrow}
→
:::
:::: {.branch-pair}
::: {.node}
**new rows**

<span class="small muted">same coordinates</span>
:::
::: {.node}
**new groups**

<span class="small muted">explicit resampling</span>
:::
::::
:::::

:::: {.grid-3 style="margin-top:.72em;"}
::: {.card .accent-teal}
**Pointwise likelihood**

Response-named and row-aligned.
:::
::: {.card .accent-teal}
**Posterior prediction**

Regenerate all modeled rows, including fitted missing values.
:::
::: {.card .accent-teal}
**Semantic outputs**

Logical names resolve backend-owned physical carriers.
:::
::::

::: {.notes}
Replay is a statistical issue: refitting a factor level map, spline basis, or HSGP domain on prediction data can silently change the model. BRM records fit/apply state and makes refitting explicit. The current shared preparation drives both backend replay paths, but some Stan descriptor and draw-transport facilities remain StanBlocks-specific.
:::

## What “shared preparation” contains

<span class="appendix-badge">Collaborator appendix B</span>

:::: {.grid-2}
::: {.card .accent-teal .tight}
<span class="label demo">Program</span>

- dependency-ordered operations
- sampled declarations and deterministic assignments
- population predictors and term records
- observations, modifiers, weights, row axes
- semantic prior addresses
:::
::: {.card .accent-blue .tight}
<span class="label demo">Fitted state</span>

- factor/group coordinates
- centers, scales, knots, spline bases
- GP/HSGP domain and frequencies
- structured-term field shapes
- replay policy and dependency provenance
:::
::::

<div class="formula-box" style="margin-top:.8em;"><span class="dim">prepared expression</span> = (callable object, positional args, keyword args, axis)
<span class="dim">prepared term</span>       = (callable, source, fitted state, dependencies)
<span class="dim">prepared observation</span>= (lhs, distribution, evidence, weights, row shape)</div>

::: {.notes}
The exact private struct names may evolve; the semantic payload is the contract. Prepared expressions keep callable objects rather than reconstructing names. A distribution factory can advertise its result shape through `brm_distribution_type`, remain a real Julia call in Turing, and obtain a separate complete-call translation for Stan.
:::

## Generated backends: same intent, different geometry

<span class="appendix-badge">Collaborator appendix C</span>

:::: {.grid-2}
::: {.card .accent-blue}
<span class="status stan">StanBlocks → Stan</span>

```stan
parameters {
  vector[K] beta_pop;
  real<lower=0> sigma;
}
model {
  beta_pop ~ normal(beta_loc, beta_scale);
  y ~ normal_id_glm(X, 0, beta_pop, sigma);
}
```

Compiler-visible blocks, activity analysis, generated quantities, BridgeStan coordinates.
:::
::: {.card .accent-violet}
<span class="status turing">Turing → DynamicPPL</span>

```julia
@model function generated(plan)
    beta_pop ~ product_distribution(priors)
    mu = plan.design.matrix * beta_pop
    for i in eachindex(y)
        y[i] ~ Normal(mu[i], sigma)
    end
end
```

Native callables, submodels, DynamicPPL conditioning/prediction, Julia AD.
:::
::::

These are compact explanatory excerpts, not verbatim generated output. The executable four-pane docs are the drift-proof comparison surface. Stan may fuse eligible Gaussian population models with `normal_id_glm`; the Turing model retains its Julia distribution construction. Semantic parity is checked after mapping parameter coordinates, not by comparing source text.

## Extension seams: where a contributor works

<span class="appendix-badge">Collaborator appendix D</span>

<div class="comparison-row header"><div>Change</div><div>Shared layer</div><div>Backend work</div></div>
<div class="comparison-row"><div><strong>Callable distribution</strong></div><div>Shape trait; dependency and axis validation.</div><div>Turing often executes directly; StanBlocks adds full-call translation, density, RNG, pointwise paths.</div></div>
<div class="comparison-row"><div><strong>Structured term</strong></div><div>Typed fitted state, fields, priors, replay.</div><div>SLIC emitter and/or native Julia submodel/effect method.</div></div>
<div class="comparison-row"><div><strong>Evidence wrapper</strong></div><div>Materialized bounds/endpoints and validation.</div><div>Executable CDF/density/RNG composition per backend.</div></div>
<div class="comparison-row"><div><strong>Output</strong></div><div>Logical identity and row/group segmentation.</div><div>Physical carrier discovery and regeneration.</div></div>

<div class="card accent-amber" style="margin-top:.8em;">
<span class="label enabled">Contributor rule</span>
 Add the semantic record once; let unsupported backends refuse by dispatch. Do not claim support until density, prediction, replay, and named-output behavior are tested at the intended boundary.
</div>

::: {.notes}
For StanBlocks, the public extension seams include predictor-term, likelihood-family, prior, submodel-RHS, sampling-LHS registration, and structured group-block hooks. For Turing, implement native term/submodel methods on the same prepared record. Ordinary callables should remain ordinary callables rather than growing an admission list.
:::

## Boundaries are a product feature {.boundary-slide}

<span class="appendix-badge">Collaborator appendix E</span>

:::: {.grid-3}
::: {.card .accent-coral .tight}
<span class="label boundary">Known gaps</span>

- no universal feature cross-product
- unequal output/transport surfaces
- adaptive geometry not general across terms/backends
- structured kernels need explicit shape/AD contracts
- several replay geometries remain fail-closed
:::
::: {.card .accent-amber .tight}
<span class="label enabled">Required evidence</span>

- construction diagnostics
- Stan compile or native model execution
- normalized density + mapped gradients
- predictive and pointwise semantics
- frozen replay and new-group behavior
:::
::: {.card .accent-violet .tight}
<span class="label research">Still research</span>

- general online geometry policy
- cross-backend equivalence criteria
- automatic marginalization
- mixed discrete/continuous structured inference
- fit portability across backend evolution
:::
::::

<div class="small muted" style="margin-top:.75em; text-align:center;">Failing loudly is part of parity: an unsupported model must not quietly acquire a different meaning.</div>

::: {.notes}
Use this slide when a collaborator asks whether the shared plan “solves” backend parity. It does not. It creates a place to state semantics once, an explicit dispatch boundary for unsupported execution, and a common target for cross-backend tests.
:::
